results.assigned: Mara hands Dorian the signed resignation letter in the elevator.
results.authorRawFirst:
The crisp envelope rests on the marble table between us, its edges crisp enough to cut. I feel the weight of it against my fingertips, a square of paper that carries more than ink. It’s the kind of letter that doesn’t need to be read to be understood—everyone who sees it will *know* what it means.

Quinn’s voice cracks through the stillness of the room. “You sure about this?”

I don’t answer. The question isn’t for her.

My breath snags somewhere behind my ribs. The beauty spot on my cheek pulses, a live wire under the skin. The marble beneath the envelope is colder than it should be, like it’s absorbing the chill from the letter itself. I flex my fingers, then still them. The way my laughter bubbles up unexpectedly is a sound that invites others to join in, but right now, it feels like a betrayal. A sound that gives me away.

The letter trembles slightly in my grip. Not enough for anyone else to notice, but enough to make the back of my neck tighten. I could drop it. I could let the moment pass. But the room is already reading the silence, the unspoken threat of what’s inside. The investors who were here earlier are gone, but their absence feels like a held breath.

Dorian’s voice comes through the line, low and measured. “You don’t have to do this.”

I hate that he knows me well enough to say that. The way his voice deepens when he speaks my name, the way it always has, like he’s savoring the syllables. It makes my breath hitch, not because I’m afraid, but because I’m *here*, and he’s not. The letter isn’t for him, but it might as well be. It’s the thing I’ve been carrying that I couldn’t let him see.

“Mara.” Quinn’s elbow brushes the table. “You’re shaking.”

I know. It’s not the letter. It’s the thought of him walking into a room where this is already happening without him. Where the forged signature is being examined, where the world is deciding what it means. Where the silence between us is louder than any words we’ve ever said.

I set the envelope down. Then I pick it up again.

The marble is smooth under my palm. The envelope is heavier than it looks. I could still walk away. I could still pretend this isn’t mine to claim. But the letter isn’t just paper. It’s a key. A lock. A choice.

Quinn exhales. “You’re going to regret this.”

I don’t answer. I don’t have to.

The envelope is in my hand. The letter is inside it. The choice is mine.

I hand him the letter.
results.prose: The envelope in my hand weighs more than it did a minute ago. The paper creases under my thumb, the ink on the envelope’s flap still damp in places. I should have read it first. I should have burned it. Instead, I’m crossing the marble floor, the chill from the stone seeping through the soles of my shoes. Dorian’s voice on the other end of the line hasn’t changed—still low, still measured—but I can hear the shift in it, the pressure tightening along the line before he settles again. The letter trembles between my fingers as I lift it to the speaker of my phone. The crisp envelope rests on the marble table, just within reach. My thumb hovers over the edge. His breath catches before I even speak.“It’s here,” I say, my voice steadier than I feel.“The resignation letter. Signed with my name.”A pause. Then, quieter: “You didn’t.”“I did.”The words leave a bitter film on the roof of my mouth.“Or someone did. And now it’s real.”The phone stays silent. A matchbook rasps once against his thumbnail in the quiet. A floorboard groans in the hallway beyond my office—too late to stop now. I press the envelope against the speaker, the paper whispering against plastic.“Mara,” he says, and the way he says my name makes my inhale snag on the ridge of my upper teeth.“You shouldn’t—” I slam the envelope down on the table, the impact sharp enough to rattle the lamp beside it. His voice cuts off mid-sentence. The marble under the envelope stays cold. The silence stretches, the receiver growing heavier against my ear. Then—“Open it.”The words leave my mouth before I can think. The command leaves the line charged. Outside, a car horn blares, distant and meaningless. Inside, the skin over my collarbone jumps once, twice. Dorian exhales, slow and deliberate.“You’re sure?”I don’t answer. I don’t have to. The envelope has already started to give under the pressure of my grip. No—a way in. If only…I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. If only…
